# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Looking for supernatural, eldritch, and/or unsettling horror movies that don't have sexual assault.

**Score:** 31
**Body:** I had posted this earlier and got a few good responses, but mods asked me to be more descriptive in the title, so I'm reposting it and hopefully this one won't get taken down 🙏

I've recently been getting into watching more horror movies, and would like some recommendations. I can handle most horror themes, but draw a hard line at sexual assault/sexual abuse, which unfortunately takes quite a few off the list. Does anyone know any horror movies without that particular theme?

The horror movies ive watched before have been Insidious (2010), Iron Lung (2026), and Ravenous (1999). Didn't really pay attention to Insidious, but I really like Iron Lung and Ravenous.

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. John Carpenter's The Thing falls under Eldritch. Classic flick 🤌🏻 
  - Carpenter's The Thing I think is the best horror movie ever made.
2. The Ritual. One of the best creatures ever put on film and no SA to worry about.  
3. Glorious.

ETA: you should check out DoesTheDogDie, it's a wonderful resource to make sure movie don't have certain triggers
4. Annihilation 
5. This is quite a combination of types of horror, some more specific to you but a lot just stuff I think someone getting into the genre may enjoy: 

Alien + Alien 2 (sci-fi horror obviously)

The Descent (a group of women go cave diving in Scotland, very claustrophobic, very well executed film)

I Saw the TV Glow (some argue this isn’t a horror film but it is, just a very allegorical and existential one)

The Ugly Stepsister (there’s some very gross/uncomfortable sex scenes but no assault, this is body horror, I’m recommending based on the vibe which you may be able to grasp by looking at a few stills)

Drag Me to Hell

The Substance (there are scenes of sexual objectification and lude sexual remarks made about different women but no assault or abuse)

The OG and 2013 remake Evil Dead films are terrible in that regard so skip those but I’d still recommend Evil Dead II (which is a remake, you don’t need to watch the first one), Army of Darkness, and Evil Dead Rise. 

Penda’s Fen (this might be my top recommendation based on your tastes, brilliant film)

Killer Klowns From Outerspace (this is a really funny film that may not be to your tastes but I recommend it to any new horror viewer)

You’re Next/The Cornetto Trilogy films/Happy Death Day (all horror comedies)

Scream (I’d check Does the Dog Die to make sure I’ve not forgotten something, I know there’s nothing on screen and none of the main kills include anything like that but it might be mentioned)

Sinners (again, check Does the Dog Die, I’ve only seen it once but I don’t think it does?)

The Stepford Wives (horror about the abuse/subjugation of women but doesn’t mention or even really imply sexual assault unless you think about it too long) 

Jennifer’s Body includes a pretty unsubtle allegory for sexual assault but none actually happens? It’s a great and pretty fun film but obviously know your boundaries

The Others (supernatural horror, it’s most definitely a horror film but one I find surprisingly cosy, I suspect you’d like it) 

The Invisible Man (remake) is great if you want a really tense and anxiety inducing horror but it’s another I have to apply a caveat to recommending because, whilst it doesn’t include sexual assault on screen or explicit mentions of it off screen, the film is about a woman leaving an abusive relationship and it is strongly implied to have occurred in the past. Again, know your boundaries.
6. Underwater 
7. The void

The endless
8. The VVitch is nice and creepy, there is a fair amount of violence but no SA 
9. Color Out of Space (2019)

## 3. Revisited “The Village.” Underrated Movie?

**Score:** 245
**Body:** My wife and I like to watch a nostalgic horror movie during Halloween. We watched The Village last night, for the first time in 20+ years for either of us. I was impressed, and don’t think it deserves its low Rotten Tomatoes score (43/57), for a few reasons (SPOILERS):

First, it has a unique and thought-provoking premise. A group of grieving adults who meet in a counseling group establish a wildlife preserve and leave society to establish a pre-modern village. They start families, and, in order to keep people from leaving, create stories about creatures in the forest who will kill them if they venture beyond the border. The premise poses interesting ethical questions. The real antagonist of the movie isn’t Noah, but the village founders (the “elders”), who are oppressing the villagers out of motivation to protect them.

Second, it’s a great love story wrapped in a horror/thriller. Ivy (Bryce Dallas Howard) traveling through the woods to save Lucius (Joaquin Phoenix), despite being blind, is super badass. The scenes where something scary is happening, and she puts out her hand, expecting Lucius to grab it, and he does, do more to establish their relationship than any amount of talking, which was great writing.

Finally, the acting, especially by the two leads, is amazing. Bryce Dallas Howard did a great job of projecting strength, but also the fear of being blind in threatening situations. 

Curious to hear people’s thoughts. M Knight gets a bad rap, but I legitimately think this is a great movie, and one of his few great ones (Sixth Sense and Unbreakable being my other two).

2. I remember enjoying this one. I don’t know why it got the hate that it did. I thought Bryce Dallas Howard was really good in it. Kept my interested the whole movie.

3. Likely based on my friend’s debut novel, Running Out of Time, without her ever receiving credit or compensation. She optioned it to Hollywood. A few years after the option expired, this movie came out. I never saw it because I’m not into spooky movies, but my wife said, “That is 100% Margaret’s novel” when she saw it in the theater. Simon & Schuster had deep pockets but not Disney deep.  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Running\_Out\_of\_Time\_(novel)#Plagiarism\_allegation
  - It was a common trope as well. I remember watching a Goosebumps episode that was very similar to 
4. Over-hyped at the time. M. Night could not escape his own shadow after Sixth Sense. I still remember certain scenes from this movie. It sticks with you. Once you see it though , I am not sure it’s worth a rewatch, which is bit true of M. Night’s other films.

6. I rewatched recently and agree with you. I think the movie is excellent. I love the nuance in the premise - it’s very human and the elders are not bad guys for keeping their secret, they’re fallible people who want to protect their loved ones from the cruelty of the world. I think every parent and person who goes through traumatic loss wants the same protection for their loved ones. The movie feels deeply human and the set design/music score are incredibly well done. It’s such a fall-time movie for me, and everything is wrapped up very well by the end!! It’s one of his most coherent films, and is quite well done in my opinion. Bryce Dallas Howard kills it, and so does Joaquin Phoenix!!

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. I think Nathan Fielder might be doing something much deeper with the Elizabeth Holmes documentary than I initially realized

**Score:** 713
**Body:** Okay, so I just finished watching this documentary and I can’t stop thinking about it lol. I actually want to watch it again, and I NEVER rewatch movies.  
At first, I genuinely felt sympathy for Elizabeth Holmes. She came across as vulnerable, somewhat socially awkward, and honestly pretty genuine. I started wondering how much of what happened with Theranos was really her doing versus the men around her controlling things.  
But the more I thought about the documentary, the more I started questioning that interpretation.  
I noticed this recurring dynamic where Elizabeth seems to present herself as this altruistic, misunderstood woman who needs protecting, and the men around her take on that protector role.  
Think about Billy. There’s that scene where she’s scrambling eggs and he literally takes over because he can do it better. Then there are the phone calls where Billy is managing her communication with Nathan, the money situation with the billboards, etc. She seems perfectly comfortable taking a backseat and letting Billy be the one in charge.  
But then you see her on business calls and she’s suddenly very competent, direct, and assertive.  
So I started wondering, is she actually this passive, vulnerable person? Or is she comfortable letting these men feel like they’re in charge because that dynamic benefits her?  
And I started thinking about how this has played out throughout her life. Her male mentor at Stanford believed in her when Phyllis Gardner questioned the science. She had all these powerful men investing in and defending her. Even her father talks about how one day people will know the real Elizabeth.  
I’m not saying women are immune to her charm or that every man falls for it. But I do wonder whether she has a particular ability to make powerful men feel like they’re protecting this brilliant, altruistic, misunderstood woman.  
And THEN there’s Amanda.  
At first I was genuinely confused about why Nathan brought Amanda into the documentary. But now I think she might be one of the most important parts of it.  
Amanda starts questioning Nathan and whether he’s becoming too sympathetic to Elizabeth. And Elizabeth seems uncomfortable with Amanda, but later has no problem speaking pretty directly about her to Nathan.  
It made me wonder whether Amanda represents a threat to the relationship Elizabeth has established with Nathan, because Amanda isn’t necessarily buying into the same narrative.  
And this is where I think Nathan might be a genius lol.  
What if Nathan is deliberately showing us what it’s like to fall for Elizabeth Holmes?  
Throughout the documentary, he seems increasingly sympathetic to her. And as an audience member, I was feeling that same sympathy! But then he gives us all these little moments that make us question what we’re seeing.  
Even that final swimming scene. Why include that? Is Nathan genuinely getting too close to his subject? Or is he purposely showing us how someone can become emotionally invested in Elizabeth’s story?  
And the craziest part is WE DON’T KNOW.  
We don’t know if Elizabeth is consciously playing this vulnerable role or if she’s genuinely that way. We don’t know if Nathan is actually falling for her or deliberately portraying himself that way. And even her father’s comments about knowing the “real Elizabeth” can be interpreted two completely different ways.  
Obviously, none of this changes the documented fraud at Theranos, and being capable and assertive doesn’t mean someone can’t also experience abuse or vulnerability. I’m talking more about how she presents herself and how the documentary makes us interpret her.  
I almost feel like the documentary isn’t just about Elizabeth Holmes. It’s about the psychology of believing Elizabeth Holmes.  
And maybe the whole point is that we leave the film questioning our own judgment.  
Am I overthinking this? 😂 Did anyone else come away with a similar interpretation? Especially the role Amanda plays and whether Nathan is intentionally making himself part of the experiment?

### Top 3 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. As I wrote in another thread: I suspect that Elizabeth thought of Nathan as a very intelligent guy who is awkward around women and therefore easy to manipulate with human warmth. The fact that he brought Amanda into play destroyed this setup. He didn’t play by Elizabeth’s and Billy’s rules. That’s why they reacted awkwardly themselves around Amanda.
  - Amanda and the dropout are also clearly a sore spot for them, as evidenced by their reaction while watching it with Nathan. They view Amanda as the villain in their story
    - Bringing Amanda in was brilliant. Seeing Elizabeth's reaction to her portrayal in The Dropout was priceless. I also really appreciated that she called Billy out on his bullshit and voiced her skepticism to Nathan about Elizabeth's believability.
      - I watched in a mostly empty theater with maybe six people. The couple behind me were talking audibly to each other about Billy throughout the first two hours of the film--how he's a manipulative narcissist, secretly gay, a total creep, snickering at him, etc. Up until the point where he starts going off about Charlie Kirk and Amanda responds that Kirk is a "pussy." They suddenly shut up, sat silently through the next scene, then said "this is a waste of time," got up and walked out. 
      - Amanda is us.
  - Elizabeth barely encountered Amanda though, right? The only time they spoke was over the phone, and Amanda felt bad that she was using Elizabeth's precious phone time.

As for Billy, I'm pretty sure Nathan felt the same way about him that the audience does. Everybody hates Billy lol.
2. I think that's absolutely what the filmmakers are driving at here, by ending the film with   
1. Nathan re-interpreting what he wrote in his script for Amanda, on the spot, to make it more sympathetic to her  
2. Amanda (audience surrogate) questioning his motivation  
3. Final reveal of swimming scene, which - earlier in the film - we were absolutely led to believe he thought the offer was too friendly / inappropriate.  He is interviewing her for a motion picture and there are no microphones there.

Ultimately this isn't a film about Elizabeth Holmes, it's a  film about the process of THIS film being made.   You Can See Everything about how it's done, but it's still a magic trick.   Including a mid-to-late film reveal of a power struggle between the subjects and its makers over money and control. 

Elizabeth is a con artist who keeps the mask on the whole time  
Billy is a con artist not clever enough to fool Nathan, or us, from the very first time he's interviewed  
Nathan is a con artist who says "I'm conning you, look, here's how".
  - I thought the David Blaine story was such a fascinating glimpse into Nathan’s psyche. I think he was essentially saying I’m conning you intellectually by deliberately losing myself emotionally in this process. Nathan’s approach is so effective because on some levels it *is* real.
    - I never thought of it like that, but I think you’re totally right. Nathan sees himself as a magician in a sense, but part of the trick is pretending he’s bad at the trick. Like Colombo. I think the spell wore off when she went to prison and he no longer had access, and the ‘real’ Nathan shone through very clearly in that scene where he recruited Seyfried, saying that he didn’t want to let her get away with playing him.

I think the reason he included that Blaine dialogue was for a different reason though. He brought up the question about why she would choose him in the first place, and towards the end he answers it through that anecdote. She wants to present herself as a misunderstood and well meaning person. Through the lens of David Blaine ‘tricking’ the audience into thinking he’s stabbed himself with an ice pick by literally doing exactly that, he’s giving her the framing she’s asking for. That she tricked people into believing in her product by literally making (or believing she made) the product. As soon as she heard that she hired him on the spot. 

This also makes her “I take things too literally and I’m too honest” claim doubly incredible, because that was a pretty complicated metaphor to parse.
  - Most movies function by trying to put the audience “behind the eyes” of the main character. You Can See Everything does this as well but for Nathan. We see how Elizabeth can manipulate by creating this narrative about herself, and the genuineness and consistency really convinces Nathan. We see the manipulation happening in real time. 

I think Nathan had a hard time accepting that she was being manipulative because he thought “there is no way she is this good of an actor”. He trusted his instincts that she was telling the truth in certain situations. 

However, the best liars convince themselves they are telling the truth. When they lie, they aren’t really lying and there are no external tells because they actually believe it is the truth. Elizabeth had convinced herself she really did nothing wrong and it was a teensy little misunderstanding. 

We are brought along on the same journey Nathan went on. You Can See Everything is actually a joke in and of itself. Elizabeth is using this documentary time to make her case, and everything we see is white washed for her to look good (she is actively doing this during the movie). Anytime something comes up Billy and Elizabeth don’t want, oh suddenly we shouldn’t be having this conversation, or the interview has to end, etc. You Can See Everything….We Want You To See is really what’s happening. Brilliant film

## 2. Major filmmakers who have notable works/achievements in other fields

**Score:** 43
**Body:** Today thinking about how Danny Boyle designed the opening ceremony of the 2012 Olympics, and had a lot of success with the stage show of Frankenstein, which (at the time) were pretty big deals and not something you would ever know existed if you were just going off his IMDB page. 

It made me think of big directors like Welles, Schnabel, McDonagh etc. who are hugely accomplished and influential outside the world of film. Can anyone point to some other interesting multi-talented filmmakers?

Would be particularly interested in ones who had achievements outside of the arts.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I feel like comedy and playwrighting is a little too adjacent to film to count. So I’ll branch out a bit more:

Tom Ford: primarily a fashion designer obviously.

George Miller was an ER doctor which I find pretty impressive 

Bob fosse - choreographer
  - Yup! And it was Miller’s experience with car accident trauma that inspired Mad Max. 
2. Terrence Malick is a Harvard-educated philosopher and was a Rhodes Scholar at Oxford. He taught philosophy at MIT before deciding to pursue filmmaking.

An incredibly clever and talented man.
  - I was going to bring up Ethan Coen but that's way more impressive
3. He’s definitely more known for his books than for his directing, but Michael Crichton directed several movies, including Westworld (1973), the Great Train Robbery (1978), and Looker (1981). He also co-wrote several adaptations of his works, like Jurassic Park and Rising Sun. He also created the television show ER.
  - Same can be said for William Peter Blatty (author of the Exorcist) who directed the massively underrated Ninth Configuration and The Exorcist III
4. James Cameron is an inventor whose contributions include: a propulsion device for swimmers, camera technologies, a submarine for one person which made him an expert at the implosion trial, other mini deep water cameras and vehicles….

I thought he was going to be your main example tbh. 

Jordan Peele was a major comedian before becoming a director. 

Satyajit Ray was influenced by the bengal renaissance so he is another example of someone whose creative outputs weren’t limited to cinema. 
5. Charlie Chaplin: music composition

Woody Allen: jazz clarinet

Stanley Kubrick: photography

Akira Kurosawa: painting

David Lynch: painting and other visual art

Steve McQueen: visual art

John Huston: boxing
6. Visconti was one of the most important figures in Italian Opera and music in general in the 1950s, Maria Callas is the obvious example and how he directed her in a lot of important productions, but he also semi-revived bel canto opera and Verdi, like La Traviata, Il trovatore and Falstaff. Besides Callas he worked with a lot of important conductors like Bernstein and singers. La Scala Opera House in Milan has an exhibit right now dedicated to Visconti's efforts and productions to remember 50 years of his passing. It's tough to say whether opera would be "dead" without him but he brought new relevance to it for the public. 

(In fact, when La Fenice opera house burned down, to rebuild it the builders used frames from Visconti's Senso since the film opens in La Fenice to make sure they built it back faithfully). 
7. To be fair, a lot of film directors have a background in stage directing. It's not uncommon at all. 

Anyway: Jean Cocteau was skilled at virtually every kind of art, with film just one of them.

## 3. Films/scenes with great writing let down by bad acting?

**Score:** 30
**Body:** When people are discussing bad films/bad scenes, it's often said that X scene or film was acted by the actor as well as they could, but the writing was just atrocious and dragged it down.  This is of course a real phenomenon and there are many instances of actors doing the best they can with a poor script, but I also feel this is often said as a kind of cop-out- people feel more comfortable criticising a director/writers because they're sort of faceless, so make excuses for actors.  Therefore I thought it would be fun to flip the cliche around- are there any films that you've watched and thought 'wow this script is amazing but the way the actor's delivering it is mediocre' or indeed 'this script could be just fine but the actor is making the scene terrible'?  Who would you have cast instead to execute the writers' vision?

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Considering the Psycho remake in 1998 is virtually the exact same script as the original film, hard to fault the dialogue. Vince Vaughn is just horribly miscast and unconvincing as twisted, vulnerable mamas boy.
  - Julianne Moore was good in it, though.

## 4. My thoughts about Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s “Evil Does Not Exist” (2023)

**Score:** 16
**Body:** (Spoilers for the film ahead)

I am a huge Hamaguchi fan. I love Passion (his first film, hidden gem), Happy Hour, Wheel of Fortune, Drive My Car, Asako I & II… So now I watched this most recent work from him (with a bit of a delay), and there were some things I really enjoyed and others that made me feel a bit unsatisfied.

I really missed watching his cinematography style, his story pace and the style of his dialogue, so in those aspects this was wonderful to me. My favourite scene was the driving part where Takahashi and Mayuzumi were talking about their passions and objectives for life. I love those types of dialogue in Hamaguchi’s films, they allow to learn and sympathize (or empathize) with the characters so much. The scene where they discussed the gampling project with the villagers also resembled a lot with the book presentation act in Happy Hour, which I really enjoyed.

Hamaguchi and his team always did a wonderful job in showing shots of Tokyo and other cities. The setting of this film, being mostly in a rural area (and especially with the winter roughness), was a sharp contrast, that made me miss the urban landscapes, which only appeared for a few seconds. Nonetheless, the cinematography was beautiful.

Another aspect is that Hamaguchi was always good at doing very intricate stories, where every character has a huge depth. Each dialogue in his films feels so rich, that makes an antagonist (like one of the boyfriends in Happy Hour) an actually understandable and complex chatacter, from whom you can empathize. These human and existential dramas, mostly regarding love, family and the doubt of self-fulfillment, really embedded well with the urban theme that existed in most of his films, where you felt the contact with different characters and the familiarity of their feelings and challenges in life.

Evil Does Not Exist doesn’t portray that theme as much, as it happens in an isolated rural area with much less things going on. The story allowed to show us more about Takahashi and Mayuzumi, you could sense a development going on, but then the ending… it felt too rushed, maybe too blunt or symbolic, in a shocking way, not really frequent from what I saw in his other films. Usually, Hamaguchi leaves us more in open endings, or at least in endings where you get as much lost in the character’s thoughts as themselves.

I saw very good critiques and reviews from this film, but that ending made it feel a bit more lackluster compared to his previous films. However, that is my view based on my own tastes, because I’m well aware that is still a great film with still an interesting story.

### Top 4 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I like this film a whole bunch and its ending makes it. One of the hardest things to do in art is to communicate a truly esoteric idea without it being obvious or heavy-handed. Hamaguchi achieves that with such an unexpected subtlety that it’s basically magic. The film is immediately and explicitly about the environment and modern corporate destruction but the way it arrives at its thesis and point is wholly unexpected. It is a moving statement about the costs and human emotion behind the forces of destruction but it pulls off the impossible: an inevitable conclusion that feels surprising. The ending seems to come out of nowhere but the more the movie sits after it closes the more perfect and inevitable the conclusion seems.

The movie doesn’t hide the views of any of its characters. The movie has no real twist. So why does it feel so shocking? My conclusion is because Hamaguchi is so smart at doing exactly what is being done to his characters: trapping us inside the rules of society. Just as his villagers wage their war within the paramaters and terms set by their corporate enemies, Hamaguchi lulls us into thinking his film is going to play by those same rules. People stick to the process even if it leads to destruction. People stay civil because that is morally right. Good people don’t act out violently. The film captures the exact idea of social society that is probably plaguing the world right now: it’s better to lose by sticking to the rules than win by breaking them. And as we watch the villagers win their small battles, while on the road to inevitable defeat, we think like they do—no one here is going to go outside the rules. So when one of the characters breaks and decides he is done we are shocked by it. There is no reason he wouldn’t do what he does but it never occurs to us because we are ourselves committed to the rule set. By breaking that, Hamaguchi challenges our entire world view and makes us ask why we are so committed to self destruction in the name of social order. It’s deeply unsettling but genius: the perfect portrait of our current extinction era civility. It’s not an optimistic film; it’s a damning one.

The other trick Hamaguchi pulls is one of form. He shoots the film like a pseudo-documentary travelogue. The film’s digital look is somewhere between nature videos on Youtube and Instagram influencer hiking videos. It has a very beautiful, crisp, real feel to it that only digital can capture. It feels almost low stakes because of that style—we do not expect a hiking video to challenge us. These formal decisions further our comfort and commitment to the rules of society. We think we know what we are seeing. But there are also subtle hits in how Hamaguchi moves and composes people. The way people move or don’t move is particularly interesting as it challenges the natural aura of the image. Much has been made of the school yard scene with frozen children but the same is true of the walks through the woods (especially their length) and numerous shots of individuals alone in the frame. The movie is hinting at what is possible: unnatural, out-of-world actions that break the fake comfort we want.
